demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Maladaptive Strategies.value: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping

Memory.value: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.

Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.explanation: For trauma type 'unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one', the body-focused appraisals 'I can no longer trust my own body' and 'I feel ashamed of what happened to my body' are hard to reconcile clinically unless the patient also directly experienced major bodily violation/injury, which is not reflected elsewhere in the profile.

The memory items imply vivid sensory reliving of the traumatic event ('hear things ... heard during the frightening event') and fragmented visual snapshots, which can occur in PTSD, but here they are not well matched to the selected appraisals: the profile centers on bodily shame/unreliability rather than grief/death-related meanings of the event.

'Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study' is not impossible, but in this profile it appears weakly integrated: there are no trigger or threat items tying work contexts to the trauma, and the formulation does not include trigger/threat pathways. The coping profile otherwise concerns sleep delay and undereating, so work avoidance feels insufficiently anchored.

issues.item: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: For trauma involving the unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, body-focused shame is clinically hard to reconcile unless there was also direct bodily violation, injury, or assault. The rest of the profile centers grief-related loss, meaning, and intrusive memory phenomena, so this item appears inconsistent with the trauma type and with the other selected items.

vignette: Talia, a 46-year-old forensic analyst from a small coastal town, found herself grappling with an unshakable sense of loss that began when her younger sister, Mia, died unexpectedly in a car accident. The news shattered Talia’s world, leaving her unable to comprehend how a life so full of potential could end so abruptly. In the months following Mia's death, Talia experienced a profound shift in her perception of life and relationships; she felt abandoned by the universe. This loss strained her faith in people and the idea that life held any inherent meaning. Talia had come to believe that her grief reflected a weakness within her, and so she avoided confronting her emotions, thinking that doing so was the only way to cope with a reality that felt unbearable. As Talia's negative appraisals deepened, she began to see herself as fundamentally flawed and incapable of handling her grief; this belief led her to conclude that avoiding her responsibilities was the only sensible choice. In her mind, the more she avoided her work and her feelings, the more it confirmed her belief that she was indeed weak and unable to cope, a conviction that intensified her feelings of inadequacy. "Nothing feels meaningful anymore," she would often say, reflecting her belief that her sister’s absence had destroyed the very fabric of her existence. As Talia’s negative appraisals deepened, she began to withdraw from her work at the forensic lab. She believed that her grief made her weak and incapable, leading her to think that avoiding her responsibilities was the only sensible choice; if she couldn't manage her feelings in a demanding environment, she must be fundamentally flawed. The thought of returning to her job felt insurmountable; she feared that the intensity of her grief would overwhelm her in a professional environment that demanded precision and focus. But each time she opted to stay away from work, her negative self-assessment deepened, reinforcing the belief that she was incapable of managing her responsibilities and further driving her to withdraw. Talia started to avoid work altogether, spending her days in a haze of regret and self-recrimination. The more she withdrew, the more vivid the memories of her sister's death became; by steering clear of her grief, she inadvertently kept the haunting recollections close, amplifying their emotional weight. Each time she opened her laptop to review case files, memories of the accident flooded back, accompanied by vivid auditory recollections of the sirens and the frantic voices of responders. Those memories struck her like a wave, leaving her breathless and helpless. This avoidance strategy not only kept her from her work but also reinforced her feelings of inadequacy and despair, further embedding her belief that her life had been irrevocably destroyed. Each time she chose to retreat from confronting her grief, she found herself spiraling deeper into self-doubt, convinced that if she were truly capable, she would be able to face her responsibilities without fear. Each time she chose to retreat instead of face her tasks, it silently affirmed her belief that she was powerless, deepening her conviction that she was incapable of moving forward. The memories of the accident haunted Talia, manifesting as fragmented snapshots that replayed in her mind like a broken film reel. Her persistent avoidance of confronting these memories meant that they remained vivid and undisturbed, amplifying their emotional weight and keeping her trapped in a cycle of distress. Each moment felt like a picture she could not erase—an image of Mia laughing, the sound of tires screeching, and the piercing sirens that followed. Each recollection overwhelmed her with emotion, making it impossible to focus or sleep. To cope, Talia began to stay up late, engaged in mindless scrolling through social media, hoping to distract herself from the memories that clung to her. Yet, each moment spent avoiding her feelings and her grief only reinforced her negative beliefs about herself, as she concluded that if she were truly strong, she wouldn't need these distractions to cope. The late nights turned into a ritual, a way to escape the emotional turmoil that surged within her whenever she closed her eyes. However, her avoidance only served to keep the memories fresh; the longer she stayed away from confronting them, the more vivid and overwhelming they became when they finally surfaced. As the months dragged on, Talia’s eating habits deteriorated. The act of preparing meals felt like a betrayal to the memory of her sister, and she found herself undereating or avoiding food altogether. Each bite felt heavy with guilt, as if she were somehow diminishing the importance of Mia's life by nourishing her own. As Talia continued to restrict her food intake to avoid facing the implications of her sister's death, she interpreted her inability to care for herself as further evidence of her inadequacy, reinforcing her negative beliefs about her worth. The combination of avoidance strategies—skipping work, delaying sleep, and restricting food—created a cycle that left Talia feeling increasingly isolated. She began to believe that she was beyond help, further solidifying her sense of hopelessness and despair. The more she engaged in avoidance strategies, the more convinced she became that she was fragile and unable to cope, which only amplified her feelings of hopelessness and solidified her negative self-image. Talia's life felt like a series of fragmented moments, each echoing the trauma of her sister's death. The more she tried to escape the memories, the stronger their hold became. Every memory reinforced her negative appraisals, and every avoidance behavior fed back into her feelings of worthlessness. By choosing to avoid confronting her grief, Talia inadvertently kept the traumatic memories fresh, making them more vivid and overwhelming each time they resurfaced. "Each time she retreated into avoidance, it silently confirmed her fears that she was weak and incapable, feeding back into her negative beliefs about herself and her future." "I don’t know what to do anymore; it feels like my life is on pause," she lamented when she finally sought help, her voice thick with sorrow. In that moment, Talia realized she could no longer navigate her grief alone. She was terrified of confronting the flood of emotions she had long avoided, yet she hoped for a way to reclaim her life and find meaning once again, even if that path seemed daunting. "The belief that life was inherently meaningless made her memories of Mia's death sharper, as if each painful recollection served to confirm her conviction that she was abandoned to a fate she couldn't control." "The effort she put into avoiding her responsibilities only deepened her conviction that she was incapable of facing reality, leading her to believe that if she were truly strong, she wouldn’t need to hide from her grief." "She had been avoiding the memories for so long that when they surfaced, they were more vivid and overwhelming than ever, each one laden with the weight of her unresolved emotions and beliefs of inadequacy." Each time she retreated instead of facing her tasks, it silently affirmed her belief that she was powerless, deepening her conviction that she was incapable of moving forward.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies: The vignette does not convey how Talia's negative appraisals lead to her maladaptive strategies.
  e.g. "If she had concluded that the world was dangerous and she was defenceless, staying home wasn't avoidance — it was the only rational thing to do."
  e.g. "The belief that speaking about it would make things worse kept her silent in her sessions, offering fragments instead of the whole picture."
  e.g. "Having decided that her feelings couldn't be trusted, she worked hard to stay numb — and had become quite good at it."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Memory: The vignette fails to establish how Talia's maladaptive strategies influence her memory of the traumatic event.
  e.g. "She had been avoiding any mention of it for so long that when the memory finally surfaced, it was louder than it had ever been — all that suppression had kept it fresh."
  e.g. "Not talking about it meant the memory had never been put anywhere; it remained in her, undisturbed and intact, exactly where she had left it."
  e.g. "The effort of keeping it at a distance had paradoxically kept it close — she had thought about not thinking about it every day for three years."
- Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals: The vignette does not demonstrate the relationship where Talia's maladaptive strategies reinforce her negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Three years of avoiding it had told her something she couldn't easily argue with: that she must be more fragile than other people, or she would have been over this by now."
  e.g. "Each time she used a safety behaviour to get through the day, she felt the quiet accumulation of evidence that she couldn't cope without it."
  e.g. "The fact that she still needed to do all of this — the checking, the planning, the long way round — confirmed, in some wordless way, that she wasn't getting better."

vignette_attempts.vignette: Talia, a 46-year-old forensic analyst from a small coastal town, found herself grappling with an unshakable sense of loss that began when her younger sister, Mia, died unexpectedly in a car accident. The news shattered Talia’s world, leaving her unable to comprehend how a life so full of potential could end so abruptly. In the months following Mia's death, Talia experienced a profound shift in her perception of life and relationships; she felt abandoned by the universe. This loss strained her faith in people and the idea that life held any inherent meaning. As Talia's negative appraisals deepened, she began to see herself as fundamentally flawed and incapable of handling her grief; this belief led her to conclude that avoiding her responsibilities was the only sensible choice. In her mind, the more she avoided her work and her feelings, the more it confirmed her belief that she was indeed weak and unable to cope, a conviction that intensified her feelings of inadequacy. "Nothing feels meaningful anymore," she would often say, reflecting her belief that her sister’s absence had destroyed the very fabric of her existence. As Talia’s negative appraisals deepened, she began to withdraw from her work at the forensic lab. She believed that her grief made her weak and incapable, leading her to think that avoiding her responsibilities was the only sensible choice; if she couldn't manage her feelings in a demanding environment, she must be fundamentally flawed. The thought of returning to her job felt insurmountable; she feared that the intensity of her grief would overwhelm her in a professional environment that demanded precision and focus. Talia started to avoid work altogether, spending her days in a haze of regret and self-recrimination. The more she withdrew, the more vivid the memories of her sister's death became; by steering clear of her grief, she inadvertently kept the haunting recollections close, amplifying their emotional weight. Each time she opened her laptop to review case files, memories of the accident flooded back, accompanied by vivid auditory recollections of the sirens and the frantic voices of responders. Those memories struck her like a wave, leaving her breathless and helpless. This avoidance strategy not only kept her from her work but also reinforced her feelings of inadequacy and despair, further embedding her belief that her life had been irrevocably destroyed. Each time she chose to retreat from confronting her grief, she found herself spiraling deeper into self-doubt, convinced that if she were truly capable, she would be able to face her responsibilities without fear. Each time she chose to retreat instead of face her tasks, it silently affirmed her belief that she was powerless, deepening her conviction that she was incapable of moving forward. The memories of the accident haunted Talia, manifesting as fragmented snapshots that replayed in her mind like a broken film reel. Each moment felt like a picture she could not erase—an image of Mia laughing, the sound of tires screeching, and the piercing sirens that followed. Each recollection overwhelmed her with emotion, making it impossible to focus or sleep. To cope, Talia began to stay up late, engaged in mindless scrolling through social media, hoping to distract herself from the memories that clung to her. Yet, each moment spent avoiding her feelings and her grief only reinforced her negative beliefs about herself, as she concluded that if she were truly strong, she wouldn't need these distractions to cope. The late nights turned into a ritual, a way to escape the emotional turmoil that surged within her whenever she closed her eyes. However, her avoidance only served to keep the memories fresh; the longer she stayed away from confronting them, the more vivid and overwhelming they became when they finally surfaced. As the months dragged on, Talia’s eating habits deteriorated. The act of preparing meals felt like a betrayal to the memory of her sister, and she found herself undereating or avoiding food altogether. Each bite felt heavy with guilt, as if she were somehow diminishing the importance of Mia's life by nourishing her own. The combination of avoidance strategies—skipping work, delaying sleep, and restricting food—created a cycle that left Talia feeling increasingly isolated. She began to believe that she was beyond help, further solidifying her sense of hopelessness and despair. Talia's life felt like a series of fragmented moments, each echoing the trauma of her sister's death. The more she tried to escape the memories, the stronger their hold became. Every memory reinforced her negative appraisals, and every avoidance behavior fed back into her feelings of worthlessness. By choosing to avoid confronting her grief, Talia inadvertently kept the traumatic memories fresh, making them more vivid and overwhelming each time they resurfaced. "Each time she retreated into avoidance, it silently confirmed her fears that she was weak and incapable, feeding back into her negative beliefs about herself and her future." "I don’t know what to do anymore; it feels like my life is on pause," she lamented when she finally sought help, her voice thick with sorrow. In that moment, Talia realized she could no longer navigate her grief alone. She was terrified of confronting the flood of emotions she had long avoided, yet she hoped for a way to reclaim her life and find meaning once again, even if that path seemed daunting. "The belief that life was inherently meaningless made her memories of Mia's death sharper, as if each painful recollection served to confirm her conviction that she was abandoned to a fate she couldn't control." "The effort she put into avoiding her responsibilities only deepened her conviction that she was incapable of facing reality, leading her to believe that if she were truly strong, she wouldn’t need to hide from her grief." "She had been avoiding the memories for so long that when they surfaced, they were more vivid and overwhelming than ever, each one laden with the weight of her unresolved emotions and beliefs of inadequacy." Each time she retreated instead of facing her tasks, it silently affirmed her belief that she was powerless, deepening her conviction that she was incapable of moving forward.
